title: Wavelength-Resolved Control of Photovoltaic Screening and Defect-Mediated Doping in Photo-Ferroelectric/Graphene Devices
authors: Krishna Prasad Maity, Mohd Uvais, Jean-Francois Dayen, Bernard Doudin, Roman Gumeniuk, Bohdan Kundys
abstract: Ferroelectrics enable large charge doping of two-dimensional overlayers, but the coexistence of switching and nonswitching charge dynamics complicate electro-optical analysis. Here, we investigate the optoelectronic response of a ferroelectric/graphene device under 365 and 530 nm illumination, disentangling effects on ferroelectric dipole alignment from extrinsic current pathways. Graphene acts as a high-gain sensor, amplifying subtle polarization dynamics into a pronounced resistance difference. By resolving switching and nonswitching channels in dark and illuminated conditions, we reveal a competition between photovoltaic charge screening and defect-assisted excitation that governs device electrostatics. Above-band gap illumination generates free carriers that induce leaky ferroelectric hysteresis and suppress the graphene resistance ratio between opposite remanent polarization states from 290% to 15% due to dynamic photovoltaic charge screening. In contrast, 530 nm illumination primarily induces charge redistribution in ferroelectrics via defect-state excitation, leading to a significantly weaker suppression of the resistance variation of graphene. These results establish practical guidelines for selecting photon energy and intensity to either preserve remanent polarization while tuning channel doping or deliberately reconfigure polarization through optical programming.
summary: This research characterizes how light controls the electrostatics of ferroelectric/graphene devices. By comparing UV and green light illumination, the authors distinguish between free-carrier-induced screening and defect-mediated charge redistribution. This provides practical guidelines for using light to either tune doping or deliberately reconfigure the ferroelectric polarization state.
main_problem: The study investigates the optoelectronic response of ferroelectric/graphene devices to disentangle the effects of ferroelectric dipole switching from extrinsic current pathways under illumination.
main_result: Above-band gap UV illumination causes dynamic photovoltaic charge screening, significantly suppressing the graphene resistance ratio, whereas sub-band gap green light causes only weak, defect-mediated charge redistribution.
method: The authors performed I-V measurements and analyzed ferroelectric hysteresis loops under dark, UV (365 nm), and green (530 nm) illumination, employing compensation techniques for leakage and stray capacitance.
model_or_system: The physical system is a ferroelectric material (e.g., PMN-PT) interfaced with a graphene overlayer. The analysis focuses on the interplay between polarization switching, photovoltaic charge screening, and defect-assisted doping.
key_observables: Graphene resistance variation ($\Delta R$), ferroelectric hysteresis loop shape, photovoltaic current, and the ratio of resistance between opposite remanent polarization states.
important_parameters: Illumination wavelength (365 nm vs 530 nm), free carrier generation (above-band gap), and charge screening magnitude (e.g., $290\%$ down to $15\%$).
main_assumptions: The analysis requires compensating for background leakage current and stray capacitance to accurately isolate intrinsic ferroelectric switching and photovoltaic effects.
figures_summary: Figures compare FE loops and graphene resistance variations under UV vs. green light; supporting figures detail the subtraction of leakage/capacitance and quantify the PV current difference.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the device response by first establishing baseline measurements (dark), then comparing the strong photoresponse induced by UV light (free carriers/screening) against the weaker, gradual response from green light (defect excitation), while rigorously compensating for parasitic electrical effects.
why_interesting: The work demonstrates how external light fields can be used to precisely control the polarization state and doping level in ferroelectric interfaces, offering a mechanism for optically writing ferroelectric memory states.
